title: Setting poems to music
sentences: Yes, as far as I remember, that one is from the debut collection, isn't it, that text—not that it matters so much,
but I do wonder a bit how you found the texts you wanted to set to music?
No, I mean, I just read—I think I had that poetry collection and I just read it
and then I also thought, or something like that.
Setting a melody to a poem is an exercise that's difficult,
or it very often isn't that successful—we have to be that honest.
Yes, how so, because?
No, I often think you can hear
or that it gets a bit like—it's hard to make it sit right, but anyway
That you can hear there was a textual original, in a way,
that the text wasn't created together with the music?
Yes, that it becomes a bit layer upon layer of things,
but now and then you get it to work, and I tried a lot of Hofmo poems just then,
and I feel really that there was only one I got right, and that's one called There Is No Everyday Anymore,
Which we recorded—the band I play in is called Valkyrien Allstars, and we still play that song,
and the one I played just now we play as well,
but we play that one in a kind of springar rhythm.
Now I just played an ordinary waltz for the occasion.
But, well, there's something about it, right, something, right,
that melody-poem, it just sits there, and it's a waltz in a way,
or at least for me it was quite straightforward.
But as soon as things get a bit less symmetrical and a bit more crooked like that,
then you're facing some challenges, because as soon as—
It's very easy for the melody to get in the way
of the text, and that's something I'm really fascinated by, actually,
that interplay between melody and text, how fine the line often is,
and how small things can make it work.
Yes, it's really fascinating.
But I stopped after we did those two songs,
after that I've never tried to set any more Hofmo to music,
because deep down I thought, damn, this is just stupid somehow, but—
Because you were afraid it would go wrong, or?
Yes, or I maybe felt it wasn't needed, but
but when I found out I was going to be part of this, I started reading—I have that brick of a collected edition.
I started reading in it and then I got the urge to try again,
because I think now I'm a bit more—I've grown up more than I was
when I worked with that material the first time, and maybe there's more to get from it.
Were there any particular poems you fell for, or?
Yes, there's actually a lot, a lot,
in a way—I don't have anything specific in mind, but.
No, I understand, but
But you can probably say more about that too,
because you've worked much more with the Hofmo material than I have, and it's a—
It takes a very long time often
before you land it in a place where it doesn't become worse than it was
when it just stood on the page, I think anyway.
That's true.
Maybe you could just play a bit for us now, and then you can—
Now it's really scary to play after everything you've said.
This is never going to go well, Susanna.
Then we can talk a bit, and then you can tell us a little about how you found your poems afterwards.
